rules.plain: Formal clause: for any claim `phi` over basis `B`, admissibility requires a derivation certificate `c` and checker `K` such that `K(B,c,phi)=accept`, with `strength(phi) <= strength(K(B,c,phi))`; bare assertion has bottom evidence.
rules.reader_plain: A result counts only when an independent check can reproduce it from the inputs it came from. A confident statement on its own counts for nothing.
rules.title: Derivation before assertion

rules.plain: Formal clause: trusted claims are decided by a small checker `K` over certificates `c`; producers emit certificates and the checker decides.
rules.reader_plain: A claim is trusted only when a small, separate check works it out again from the evidence supplied with it. The program that produced an answer never approves its own answer, however capable it is.
rules.title: Kernelized verification

rules.plain: Formal clause: `auth(subject,effect)` is derived from dereferenced tokens, policy, proof refs, and world state; ambient identity is insufficient.
rules.reader_plain: Holding a key or token gives no permission by itself. Permission is worked out for this specific action, when you take it, from the rules and the current situation.
rules.title: Authority by derivation, not possession

rules.plain: Formal clause: for derived artifact `a=f(B)`, identity is `H(B)`; equal basis may reuse, basis drift forces recompute, and missing basis is bottom.
rules.reader_plain: A stored result can be reused only when the exact inputs it was built from are unchanged; a matching name or location is not enough. If the inputs changed it must be rebuilt, and if they cannot be found there is no result.
rules.title: Content-addressed determinism

rules.plain: Formal clause: `status(composite)=meet(status(parts))`; no evidence defaults to blocked, and later stages may lower but not raise authority without a new derivation.
rules.reader_plain: Something built from parts is only as trusted as its weakest required part. A part with no evidence counts as blocked, and a later step can lower trust but never quietly raise it.
rules.title: Fail-closed monotone lattice

rules.plain: Formal clause: `not_proven(P)` does not imply `proven(not P)`; coverage is closed-world only inside declared finite domains.
rules.reader_plain: Finding no evidence for something differs from showing it is false. You can call an absence a "no" only inside a list you have checked completely; otherwise the honest answer is "unknown".
rules.title: Open-world epistemics

rules.plain: Formal clause: a partial computation `g` is totalized as `Result`: `Ok(y)` when `Pre(x)` holds, otherwise `Refusal(reason,evidence)`.
rules.reader_plain: A calculation may return a number only when the conditions it needs actually hold. When they don't, it hands back a labelled refusal naming the reason, never a quiet number or blank that the next step reads as an answer.
rules.title: Typed partiality and refusal

rules.plain: Formal clause: data labels propagate along flows; untrusted labels reach privileged sinks only through declared transforms satisfying sink policy.
rules.reader_plain: A record of where a value came from, and how far it may travel, must follow it everywhere. Untrusted material can reach a sensitive place only after a stated cleaning step.
rules.title: Provenance propagation and non-interference

rules.plain: Formal clause: an effect requires a compensator or declared irreversible boundary; multi-step effects land as a saga with compare-and-swap and single-writer constraints.
rules.reader_plain: A change only counts as done if there is a stated way to undo it, or a clear note that it can never be undone. A change in several steps goes ahead only if its expected starting point is unchanged and nobody else is changing the same thing.
rules.title: Compensable transactional effects

rules.plain: Formal clause: claims over live state are cached reads valid only under `<value,as_of,basis,rederive>` invalidation contracts.
rules.reader_plain: A number about something that keeps changing is a reading taken at one moment. To be usable later it has to say when it was read, where it was read from and how to read it again.
rules.title: Temporal validity and freshness contracts

rules.plain: Formal clause: `authority(d)` implies `d in L(G)`, required receipt obligations, and anti-claim are present; prose alone is projection.
rules.reader_plain: A rule can govern only when it passes a fixed format check and lists the evidence it must produce and what it leaves out. A well-written paragraph on its own is something to read.
rules.title: Executable grammar before doctrine authority

rules.plain: Formal clause: for every Microcosm artifact `a`, any claim `phi` carried by `a` must satisfy the same admissibility relation as external claims.
rules.reader_plain: The system holds its own statements about itself to the same standard it holds everyone else's. Being the one doing the checking earns it no discount.
rules.title: Reflexive accountability / no privileged meta-layer

rules.plain: Treat a fixture label, a declared verdict, a route status, a count or a line of public copy as a statement to check. Recompute the verdict from the lower-level evidence, and keep a negative fixture with a deliberately wrong label, so that a check which only repeats labels fails.
rules.reader_plain: Trust a result only after working it out again from the underlying evidence, and keep a deliberately wrong test case that the check has to reject.
rules.title: Recompute, do not echo

rules.plain: A claim may say no more than the named checker, validator, registry or witness route actually computes. If the checker decides only a local contract, describe the result as that local contract and nothing wider.
rules.reader_plain: A statement can only be as strong as the exact thing the check settled. If a check confirms one small, local fact, the writing around it must stay at that size.
rules.title: Lower claim strength to checker strength

rules.plain: Let a small verifier, parser, harness, compiler route, registry contract or kernel decide what is trusted, in place of a broad written account of why a result looks right. The code that produces results may be large; the code that decides should be small enough for a person to read and rerun.
rules.reader_plain: Put your trust in one small, simple step that redoes the work and decides. The large, complicated program that produced the answer stays out of that decision, because the thing being judged should not judge itself.
rules.title: Concentrate trust in small checkers

rules.plain: Permission to change something comes from the referenced proof, policy, result record and rollback evidence, each opened and checked, together with the current state of the repository. A credential, a role name, administrator wording or a phrase such as "trusted session" is never enough on its own to authorize a change.
rules.reader_plain: Holding a credential, having a role name or being in a 'trusted' session gives no permission to change anything by itself. Permission is worked out again for each action, from the rules and the current situation.
rules.title: Possession is not permission

rules.plain: A saved result, command output, source import or work-landing attempt that may be reused must record a hash of the exact content it was computed from. Any change to the source bytes, to uncommitted files in its scope, to the parent commit or to the fixture input means it has to be recomputed.
rules.reader_plain: A saved result can be reused only if it is tagged with the exact inputs it was made from and those inputs still match. If the inputs have changed, the work has to be redone, whatever the name or label says.
rules.title: Cache by content, not by name

rules.plain: A missing piece of evidence, policy file, source digest, secret scan, negative case or self-scan of a result record blocks the result or lowers its status. A generated summary further downstream can explain why something passed, and it can never turn a blocked source into a pass.
rules.reader_plain: A combined result is only as sound as its weakest part. If one part has no evidence behind it, the whole counts as not ready. A later step can downgrade that verdict, and raising it takes fresh work.
rules.title: Status fails closed

rules.plain: A coverage report names the domains it declared and the gaps it found inside them. Anything outside those domains stays unknown, and the report must never describe it as safe, complete, exhausted or irrelevant.
rules.reader_plain: A coverage report can only speak about the area it actually checked, and it has to name that area and the gaps it found. Anything outside the area is unknown.
rules.title: Track known unknowns without claiming the unknown is mapped

rules.plain: When a precondition fails, return a refusal that gives the reason. Never emit a meaningless statistic, a proof status, a safety verdict or a public-readiness status just to keep a pipeline green.
rules.reader_plain: When a step cannot be done properly because something it needs is missing, it should hand back a clear refusal that says why, instead of a made-up answer that makes the work look finished.
rules.title: Refuse inadmissible computations with typed reasons

rules.plain: Every piece of data that moves out of the private source system, a fixture, a result record, public copy, a provider's response format or material stored next to the private root must carry a label saying where it came from and how strongly it may be claimed. If the flow is only declared, or labelled only at its end, say so.
rules.reader_plain: A value carries a record of where it came from and how far it may be used, and that record travels with it through every handoff. If something was only labelled clean at the final step, that has to be written down.
rules.title: Preserve provenance across every boundary

rules.plain: Writes, release steps, releasing a claim on a path, source imports and anything that can be rolled back need evidence that their steps ran in order as one transaction. Release a lock only after the durable records are written, recompute after the release, and block a change whose parent commit is stale or whose path someone else has claimed.
rules.reader_plain: An action counts as done only when there is a permanent record of it, a way to undo it or a stated point of no return, and a check that nobody else changed the same thing at the same time from outdated information. Running without errors is not enough.
rules.title: Do not land effects without compensation

rules.plain: Counts, "current" states, live route totals, CI minimums, body-import minimums and readiness signals must say how they can be recomputed. If they cannot be recomputed, leave them out of lasting prose or mark them as snapshots with a date.
rules.reader_plain: A number about something that keeps changing, like a current count or a readiness status, may sit in a lasting document only if it says when it was read and how to work it out again. Otherwise mark it as a dated snapshot.
rules.title: Bind volatile facts to refresh routes

rules.plain: A doctrine document gains authority only when it passes the grammar, has its required fields, lists the result records it must produce and the statements of what it does not cover (its anti-claims), and has a validator that checks it. Until it has that executable contract, its prose can help a reader find their way and has no authority over the system.
rules.reader_plain: A written rule can govern other parts of the system only after a program checks its form and finds its required parts and stated limits. Well-written words alone can guide a reader and nothing more.
rules.title: Make doctrine executable before authoritative

rules.plain: Files Microcosm writes about itself get no exemptions. Its standards, paper modules, ledgers, routes, generated pages and release claims must meet the same evidence, anti-claim and refusal requirements they apply to everything else.
rules.reader_plain: When the system describes or assesses itself, that description has to meet exactly the same evidence and honesty standard it enforces on everything else.
rules.title: Apply the same floor to meta artifacts

rules.plain: The content hash records which bytes or rows were used; the provenance label records where they may go and how strongly they may be claimed. A piece of data needs both before it is fully routed.
rules.reader_plain: Every piece of data needs two tags at once, one saying exactly which inputs it was built from and one saying where it may go and how strongly it can be claimed. If either tag is missing, the data is not ready to use.
rules.title: Carry basis and provenance together

rules.plain: Generated docs, markdown summaries, route cards and paper modules may present what the source says and may never raise it. When the source content, the grammar or the source's status no longer supports a generated page, recompute the page from the source or lower its status.
rules.reader_plain: A generated page can display what a source says, but it carries no more authority than that source. If the source weakens, the page has to be regenerated or marked down.
rules.title: Keep projections below source authority

rules.plain: Permission to change a file depends on more than who has access to it. It combines permission derived from a proof, the write scope claimed for this change, the current parent commit, a way to undo the change, and evidence that this particular transaction landed.
rules.reader_plain: Permission to change something takes several conditions holding together for this exact change. You need worked-out permission, agreed limits on what you may touch, a current state that still matches what you expected, a way to undo, and a record that it landed.
rules.title: Bind authority to transaction scope

rules.plain: Before adding or removing a link between doctrine records in a registry where keys repeat, tie the change to the one source row, the target id and the builder that will read it. A generated page, a change in a count or a nearby key with the same name is no substitute for that row.
rules.reader_plain: Before adding or removing a connection in a list of relationships, point to the exact source entry that names it and the place that will use it. A similar entry nearby, or a count that went up by one, is not enough.
rules.title: Anchor graph mutations to unique source rows

rules.plain: A staged law, standard, component or generated page becomes active only when its owner boundary, source row, matching generated output, validation result record and status change have all landed in the same governed transaction, or when an explicit blocked result record records where the work stopped. If the source a page was generated from has uncommitted changes held by another active owner, the page is not yet current; ask for a handoff, wait for that owner to land the change, or write a bloc
rules.reader_plain: A new rule does not start to count just because a draft has appeared. Its owner, exact source entry, matching generated copy, passing check and recorded status change all have to land together in one step, and until then it is pending.
rules.title: Require fan-in before activation

rules.plain: A residual is a recorded, typed gap where a link might belong, and it is kept separate from the links themselves. Before wiring a missing neighbour, record the declared domain, the source row, whether the target resolves, whether the gap can be filled, the minimum evidence required, and the anti-claim. A candidate route, a neighbour suggested by generated output, a matching file name, a single match or a stale row in a generated page all remain gaps. A gap becomes a link only when the current so
rules.reader_plain: A missing link in the map is a recorded gap with a type, left open until filled properly. You draw the link only once a current source names it and the target really exists.
rules.title: Classify residual pressure before wiring

rules.plain: Generating a doctrine record's pages does not make the record active. Attach its validator result records, evidence references, omissions, anti-claims and authority limits to the record before treating its JSON, markdown, routing link or public copy as current and authoritative.
rules.reader_plain: A record does not become the trusted version just because a readable copy exists. The results of its checks, references to its evidence, what it leaves out and how far it may claim all have to be attached first.
rules.title: Bind receipts before record authority

rules.plain: Repeating a fixture verdict, registry label, markdown claim or model answer without recomputing it from the lower-level evidence.
rules.reader_plain: The mistake of repeating a stored verdict, label or model answer as if it were true, without working it out again from the evidence it should rest on.
rules.title: Fixture-label echo

rules.plain: Trusting a producer, persona, route, credential or past success where a checker, proof, policy or checked capability should decide.
rules.reader_plain: The mistake of letting something through because of who sent it, what badge it carries or that it worked last time, without checking that this request is allowed right now.
rules.title: Producer trust

rules.plain: Reading counts, handles, passing validators or evidence classes as a measure of product maturity, release readiness or whole-system correctness.
rules.reader_plain: The mistake of reading one summary number, such as how many checks passed, as if it said the whole thing is finished or ready, when parts nobody measured could still be failing.
rules.title: Rank-as-product-score

rules.plain: Reusing a cached result looked up by name, path, route, display label or producer after the content it was computed from has changed.
rules.reader_plain: The mistake of reusing a saved answer filed under a name or address after the thing behind that name has been changed or replaced.
rules.title: Cache-across-drift

rules.plain: Reading missing evidence as evidence of absence outside a declared domain in which every case was checked.
rules.reader_plain: The mistake of treating a place where nothing was found as a finding that nothing is there, when nobody may have looked, or looked everywhere.
rules.title: Unknown-unknown exhaustiveness

rules.plain: Returning a number or conclusion from a computation whose preconditions failed, where a typed refusal was required.
rules.reader_plain: The mistake of producing a number anyway when something the number depends on is missing, instead of saying 'I cannot answer this, and here is why'.
rules.title: Inadmissible number emission

rules.plain: Letting untrusted, private, provider, prompt, credential or raw-voice material reach a privileged or public destination without an origin label and a sanitizing transform.
rules.reader_plain: The mistake of letting private or untrusted material reach a public or high-trust place because the last step looked clean, without a label saying where it came from and without running it through a stated cleaning step.
rules.title: Public/private membrane breach

rules.plain: Making an irreversible change without an undo step, a rollback record, a compare-and-swap or world-version guard, or an explicit declaration that it cannot be undone.
rules.reader_plain: The mistake of making a real change that is hard to undo while assuming it can be undone, when nothing was set up to undo it and nothing checked that the situation had not already moved.
rules.title: Blind irreversible mutation

rules.plain: Writing a live fact into prose without its `as_of` date, the inputs it came from and a way to recompute it.
rules.reader_plain: The mistake of writing a changing number or a 'current' status into permanent text as if it were fixed, with no note of when it was read, where it came from or how to work it out again.
rules.title: Frozen live fact

rules.plain: Giving doctrine prose the authority of an executable rule before it passes the grammar and lists the result records it must produce.
rules.reader_plain: The mistake of treating a confidently written paragraph as a binding rule when it never went through the system's formal checks and never says what evidence it owes or where it applies.
rules.title: Prose-as-executable-authority

rules.plain: Exempting Microcosm's own result records, docs, releases, generated pages or validators from the evidence checks Microcosm applies to everything else.
rules.reader_plain: The mistake of letting the system's own pages, checkers, result records or generated views skip the evidence test it makes everything else pass, because it is the system talking about itself.
rules.title: Meta-artifact exemption

rules.plain: Using synthetic fixtures in place of real material that is available and safe to publish.
rules.reader_plain: The mistake of building a real conclusion on a made-up input when genuine, shareable material was available, so the made-up input gives the conclusion strength it never earned.
rules.title: Synthetic substrate substitution

rules.plain: Treating generated result records as if a person had written them as source.
rules.reader_plain: The mistake of treating an automatically generated summary as if it were the hand-written original, and then editing or quoting it as the source while the real source no longer matches.
rules.title: Generated-receipt source inversion

rules.plain: Letting public docs imply a hosted service, access to an external service, changes to source files, financial or trading decisions, production readiness, an affiliation or endorsement, or equivalence with the private system, when no valid witness supports it.
rules.reader_plain: The mistake of letting a public page's wording suggest powers the system does not have, such as being a hosted, ready product, having an outside partner, changing its own source, making financial decisions or being the same as the larger private system.
rules.title: Public-authority inflation

rules.plain: Using field terms such as proof, verifier, information flow, world model or benchmark integrity for a public mechanism that only checks the shape of a result record or generated page.
rules.reader_plain: The mistake of using strong words such as 'verifier' or 'world model' for something that only checks the shape of a record.
rules.title: Mechanism theater

rules.plain: Displaying a declared, inferred or generated downstream target as an effect observed at runtime, with no evidence that the effect happened.
rules.reader_plain: The mistake of showing where an action was meant to go as if it had already arrived there, when nothing checked that it reached the receiving end.
rules.title: Receiver inflation

rules.plain: Letting a markdown page, generated card, atlas row or short result summary override the executable contract it summarizes.
rules.reader_plain: The mistake of letting a generated page or summary overrule the contract it was only meant to describe.
rules.title: Projection-as-source
